current_text: Your coat goes over the chair back with the package folded into it, alongside the coat already hanging there. Two steps later you have the other coat over your arm and the door in front of you.
Two heads together at the far table, their voices kept under the room. You have no business with them yet.
Two men have the far table between them. One of them faces the room; the jug at their elbows is still full to the neck.

A name is cut into every piece somewhere — a bow stave, the spear haft, the inside of the buckler's grip. Two bows and the cracked buckler sit along the top rail, one very good spear standing under them. Not one piece carries a card from the house.
Your hat goes onto the third peg, brim out — nine hats on the rail now. Across the room a man lowers his cup an inch and holds it there, watching you do it.
One leg is a finger short of the other three. A folded playing card is wedged under it, and the stool still rocks when you touch it.
Blanket drawn flat, corners folded square. The pillow sits at the head end without a dent in it.
A Gnoll in a tailored vest, tall hat on indoors, both hands in view on the table. He looked at the door behind you before he looked at your face.
The line you take off the slate runs longer this time, out to a door further out of the way. The marker makes it three gold; without it the walk pays two.
A broad man dealing solitaire with a bowler still on his head. He squares each card to the one under it before he sets down the next.
A Gnoll on his feet beside the door, a folded coat over one arm. The coat is cut for a smaller man.
A Drake with his back to the wall, on a stool, the good shelf and the banded chest both in front of him. When you look at the chest, he is already looking at you.
Two rows of bottles, the bottom row opened and the corks shoved back in crooked. On the top row the wax over every neck is unbroken.
Shipping crates stacked waist-high against the wall, and a gap between two stacks where the dust on the top edge has been rubbed off.
Shadow under the colonnade and nobody in it. Come back when it is dark.
The glazier sets a pane on edge in the rack and puts his eye to the top edge of it, sighting down the street through the glass.
Three tables behind glass gone opaque with steam. On a slate by the door smoke-leaf is chalked at a price by the ounce and no grade beside it.

Every door standing open on this building is round the side, facing the alley. The frontage keeps one narrow door and one clean window. The board hanging over them is burgundy and brass, lettered COYLE AND SONS.
Pink lacquer and a black wheel-rim, already past the end of the colonnade by the time your head comes round. The calling starts again a beat later, one shopfront at a time down the row.
Half the barrow's load is on the pavement, half is still roped on. The porter sits on the shaft with his sleeves rolled and watches the street move past him.
A man in a mustard-brown coat passes you going east, and passes you again going west a minute later.
The crates sit flat where you left them, and the space behind the bottom one is bare paving.
One low oak wedge is taking the whole lean, shaved flat where it faces out. Pulling at the crates will not do it; working that wedge out properly might.
Jars in rows with their labels turned out, and a burner on the bench with a scorch ring under it. The card over the shelf is hand-lettered: WORKING SPACE, BY THE HOUR, NO CREDIT.
The back door has no handle on this side. You have nothing to bring through it.
The front passage narrows to one man's width, and the man is in it: fitted gray coat, hands behind him. The key on his cuff-chain hangs outside the sleeve.

Two tallies pinned to the bale, the same goods priced twice. The second carries no buyer's name — a hat and a feather inked in the corner, and under it a delivery line: the plain door at the alley's end.
Tea's on the house. Word costs a gold, and I pour that by the cup too.
Two figures in the turn where the alley bends — one standing, one crouched at the wall. Neither has moved since the alley mouth showed them to you.
Three men shoulder to shoulder across the passage, burgundy and brass at collar and cuff — Coyle's livery. Clubs and knives in their hands, and not a piece of Watch steel among them.
A line at ankle height, drawn tight from the crate to the drainpipe. The knot at the crate end is where careful hands would start.
The fire is low and the ash under the grate is deep. The nearest stacks of paper stand a hand's width off the iron.
Dust in the dome of the brass bell, a clean blotter under it, and a small mirror screwed to the shelf edge. Look into the mirror and you are looking at the doorway.
The desk sits at an angle to the window: the page faces the wall, the scribe faces the street. On the page side there is a second chair, pushed back from the desk and left at a slant.
